description: Thirteen days that brought the superpowers to the brink of nuclear war — quarantine, diplomacy, climbdown.
content_html:
Background: Cuba and the Cold War

In January 1959, Fidel Castro took power in Cuba, nationalising American businesses and accepting Soviet economic and military support. In April 1961 the USA backed an invasion by Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs, which failed humiliatingly. The episode damaged US prestige and deepened Castro’s alignment with Moscow. By mid-1962, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev had decided to station nuclear missiles in Cuba, placing them within striking distance of major American cities.

Khrushchev had several motives. He wished to deter any future US invasion of Cuba, to close the nuclear gap with the USA (the USSR had far fewer intercontinental ballistic missiles), and to use Cuba as a bargaining chip to pressure the USA into removing its Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Historians continue to debate the relative weight of these motives: some emphasise Soviet defensive logic; others emphasise Khrushchev’s willingness to take risks.

Key Fact

On 14 October 1962, an American U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet missile installations under construction in Cuba. President Kennedy was informed on 16 October. Over the next 13 days the world came closer to nuclear war than at any other point in the Cold War.

The Thirteen Days: Kennedy’s Response

Kennedy convened a secret advisory group called the ExComm. It debated options ranging from an air strike to a naval blockade. Kennedy rejected an immediate air strike — partly on moral grounds, partly because military advisers could not guarantee it would destroy all missiles. He chose a naval quarantine, carefully avoiding the legal term “blockade” (which implies an act of war).

On 22 October 1962, Kennedy addressed the American public on television, revealing the existence of the missiles and announcing the quarantine. He demanded Soviet ships carrying missiles turn back, and warned that a nuclear strike from Cuba would trigger an American response against the Soviet Union. The world watched as Soviet ships approached the quarantine line.

27 October 1962 is known as “Black Saturday”. An American U-2 spy plane was shot down over Cuba by a Soviet missile. Soviet submarines near the quarantine line received depth charges from US warships and one Soviet commander briefly considered launching a nuclear torpedo before being overruled by another officer, Vasili Arkhipov. The situation was on the edge of disaster.

A resolution came through a combination of public and secret diplomacy. Publicly, Kennedy agreed not to invade Cuba. Secretly, US Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy told Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin that the Jupiter missiles in Turkey would be quietly removed within a few months — though this concession would not be announced publicly. On 28 October 1962 Khrushchev announced the missiles would be withdrawn from Cuba.

Aftermath and the Road to Détente

The resolution of the crisis exposed how close the superpowers had come to catastrophic miscalculation. Both sides drew the same lesson: direct communication in a crisis was essential. In 1963, a direct telephone link — the Moscow–Washington hotline — was installed between the White House and the Kremlin. Later in 1963, the Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed, banning nuclear testing in the atmosphere, underwater and in space.

The secret Jupiter missile deal was only declassified after the Cold War ended. Its absence from the 1962 public record is a significant source-skills teaching point: what audiences believed at the time was not the complete picture. Post-Cold War scholarship has used Soviet and American archive releases to reconstruct the crisis more fully, showing that both sides made concessions that were not visible to the public — or to each other — at the time.

Key Fact

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 resulted in three immediate outcomes: the Soviet withdrawal of missiles from Cuba; a secret US commitment to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey; and the establishment of the Moscow–Washington hotline in 1963. The crisis accelerated the move toward limited arms control agreements.

Fidel Castro was furious at the resolution of the crisis. He had not been consulted during the back-channel negotiations and felt the Soviet Union had betrayed Cuba by agreeing to withdraw missiles without Cuban input. For Castro, the public pledge of non-invasion was insufficient compensation: the USA had already demonstrated its hostility through the Bay of Pigs. Cuba remained a source of Cold War friction for the next three decades.

For both superpowers, the crisis demonstrated the dangers of nuclear brinkmanship. It directly accelerated arms control talks and the broader shift toward détente that marked superpower relations in the late 1960s and 1970s. The lesson both sides drew — that miscalculation could produce catastrophe — shaped every subsequent Cold War confrontation.
exam_tip_html: On questions about the Cuban Missile Crisis, examiners look for students who can present multiple perspectives rather than a single narrative of “who won”. Be ready to explain Khrushchev’s motives (deterring US invasion, closing the missile gap, Turkey bargaining chip) alongside Kennedy’s choices. The secret Jupiter deal is high-value detail that answers who made concessions. Also remember: if asked about interpretations, the post-Cold War archive evidence changed what historians could say about the crisis — that shift in evidence is itself historiographically significant.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The crisis began when U-2 photographs on 14 October 1962 revealed Soviet missiles in Cuba; Kennedy chose a naval quarantine over an air strike and confronted Khrushchev on television on 22 October.
  • Black Saturday (27 October) was the most dangerous moment: a U-2 shot down, a Soviet submarine nearly launching a nuclear torpedo. A secret deal — no US invasion of Cuba plus quiet removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey — ended the crisis on 28 October.
  • The aftermath produced the Moscow–Washington hotline (1963) and the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), marking the first steps toward superpower communication and limited arms control.

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why Khrushchev placed Soviet missiles in Cuba in 1962.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed reasons, each with specific supporting detail (e.g. to deter US invasion after Bay of Pigs; to close the missile gap with the USA). Secure: Two identified reasons with some development. Developing: Two reasons identified but not developed. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis for superpower relations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed consequences with specific evidence (hotline established 1963; Partial Test Ban Treaty; both sides chastened by how close conflict came). Secure: Two consequences with supporting detail. Developing: Two consequences identified but development is limited. Emerging: One basic consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Cuban Missile Crisis was the most dangerous moment of the Cold War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument with specific evidence (Black Saturday; submarine near-launch; 13-day timeline) linked to a clear judgement. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Some explanation with limited detail. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Kennedy's response to the discovery of Soviet missiles in Cuba.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features with specific detail (e.g. naval quarantine announced 22 October; ExComm formed to consider options). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the secret Jupiter missile deal is significant for historians studying the Cuban Missile Crisis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Well-developed explanation linking the secret deal to the resolution of the crisis and to the post-Cold War opening of archives that changed historical understanding. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Brief descriptive statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why 27 October 1962 (Black Saturday) was the most critical day of the Cuban Missile Crisis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of multiple causal factors (U-2 shot down; submarine depth-charge incident; Vasili Arkhipov intervention) with clear links to how close nuclear war came. Secure: Clear explanation with evidence. Developing: Some explanation but development limited. Emerging: Brief descriptive account.

knowledge_checks.q: On which date did an American U-2 plane photograph Soviet missile installations in Cuba?
What term did Kennedy use for the naval blockade to avoid it being classified as an act of war?
The secret advisory group Kennedy assembled to manage the crisis was called _____.
The Moscow–Washington hotline was established in _____ as a direct result of the missile crisis.
Match each event to its date during the crisis:

flashcard_questions.q: When did U-2 photographs reveal Soviet missiles in Cuba?
What was the Bay of Pigs (April 1961)?
flashcard_questions.a: A failed US-backed invasion of Cuba by Cuban exiles that deepened Castro's alignment with the USSR.
The Executive Committee of the National Security Council — Kennedy's secret advisory group during the crisis.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Kennedy choose a quarantine rather than an air strike?
flashcard_questions.a: An air strike could not guarantee destroying all missiles, and would constitute an act of war with less diplomatic space.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Kennedy announce the quarantine publicly?
flashcard_questions.a: 22 October 1962, in a television address to the American public.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is 27 October 1962 called Black Saturday?
flashcard_questions.a: A U-2 was shot down over Cuba and a Soviet submarine nearly launched a nuclear torpedo before being overruled.
Soviet submarine officer who overruled a decision to launch a nuclear torpedo on Black Saturday.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the secret part of the deal that ended the crisis?
flashcard_questions.a: The USA quietly agreed to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey within a few months — not publicly announced.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the public part of the deal that ended the crisis?
flashcard_questions.a: Kennedy pledged not to invade Cuba; Khrushchev agreed to withdraw Soviet missiles.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963)?
flashcard_questions.a: A treaty signed by the USA, USSR and UK banning nuclear testing in the atmosphere, underwater and in space.
A direct telephone link established in 1963 to allow direct communication between the US President and Soviet leader in a crisis.

glossary_terms.definition: Cuban revolutionary leader who took power in January 1959, nationalised US businesses and aligned Cuba with the Soviet Union.
Soviet leader 1953–1964 who placed nuclear missiles in Cuba in 1962, triggering the most dangerous confrontation of the Cold War.
US intermediate-range ballistic missiles stationed in Turkey, seen by the USSR as a direct nuclear threat to Soviet territory.
The Executive Committee of the National Security Council, the secret advisory group Kennedy assembled to manage the Cuban Missile Crisis.
The naval blockade of Cuba announced by Kennedy on 22 October 1962, described as a quarantine to avoid the legal status of an act of war.
A high-altitude US reconnaissance aircraft; one was shot down over Cuba on 27 October 1962, raising the risk of military escalation.
US Attorney General and the President's brother, who conducted secret back-channel diplomacy with Soviet Ambassador Dobrynin during the crisis.
Soviet Ambassador to the United States who conducted secret diplomatic communications with Robert Kennedy during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
A direct telephone link established in 1963 between Washington and Moscow to allow the US President and Soviet leader to communicate directly in a crisis.
The 1963 treaty signed by the USA, USSR and UK banning nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere, underwater and in space.
